case_studies.title: LiveMem: Maintaining Memory State Continuity in Long-Running LLM Inference
case_studies.abstract: Long-running assistants and agents consume interaction streams that eventually outgrow the context. Existing context retention, summarization, and retrieval preserve access to selected history, but do not provide a persistent state over the full lifecycle when working context changes. We formulate this missing inference capability as \emph{state continuity under context turnover}: carrying computation forward through a fixed-capacity memory state whose lifetime is independent of the active context. We introduce an intrinsic memory method, \textbf{LiveMem}, which augments a pretrained full-atte
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of maintaining memory state continuity in long-running Large Language Model (LLM) inference, the team built LiveMem, an intrinsic memory method that augments pretrained models, and the result is a persistent state over the full lifecycle of working context changes. This technology is relevant to managing cloud infrastructure that uses LLMs. It improves the performance of long-running assistants and agents.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM inference workloads, here is what to do: review your current context retention and retrieval methods, consider implementing LiveMem to improve state continuity, and test its impact on your workload performance. This flags a risk: if your org uses LLMs for long-running tasks, check your current memory state management immediately. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to AI and machine learning workloads.

case_studies.title: Magnet: Detecting Cross-Session AI Misuse Through Capability Accumulation
case_studies.abstract: The most capable AI deployments are not single models but ensembles of specialized agents that delegate and act in coordination. This architecture unlocks powerful new capabilities, and it also introduces risks that existing frameworks for monitoring, detection, and mitigation were not designed to address. Most state-of-the-art AI abuse detection literature focuses on single-turn or multi-turn (single-session) threat models. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of detecting AI misuse across multiple sessions by building a system called Magnet, which resulted in improved detection of coordinated AI attacks. Magnet identifies potential threats by tracking the accumulation of capabilities across multiple AI sessions. This research aims to address a critical gap in existing AI abuse detection frameworks.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI-powered systems, here is what to do: review your current detection and mitigation frameworks to ensure they can identify cross-session threats, assess your AI architecture for potential vulnerabilities, and consider implementing a capability accumulation tracking system like Magnet. This flags a risk: if your organization uses ensemble AI models, check your security controls immediately to prevent coordinated attacks. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to AI-specific infrastructure management.

case_studies.title: Real-Time Detection and Repair of LLM Agent Failures
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents fail mid-episode -- they loop, cascade tool errors, drift off goal, fabricate results, or silently absorb corrupted content -- and the standard remedy, judging every step with a second LLM, costs more than the agent itself. We ask how much detection is achievable from observable step telemetry alone, using monitors costing microseconds per step and trained only on healthy runs. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of LLM agent failures by detecting and repairing them in real-time, the authors built a detection system using observable step telemetry, and the result shows that this approach can be effective with low costs. The system uses monitors trained on healthy runs to detect failures. This can help reduce the costs of repairing LLM agent failures.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM agent infrastructure, here is what to do: review your current failure detection methods, consider implementing a real-time detection system using observable step telemetry, and assess the costs and benefits of this approach for your organization.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper discusses real-time detection and repair of LLM agent failures which is directly relevant to IT engineers working with large language models. Novel method to detect failures and potential value in real-world deployment.

case_studies.title: AtumAI: A Principled Framework for Agentic Generation of Datacenter Control-Plane Policies
case_studies.abstract: The efficiency of a datacenter rests on its control plane policies. Designing these policies is increasingly hard: the hardware-software stack grows fast, the design space is vast and interdependent, and prototyping a single policy takes months. Agentic AI promises to automate this search. Off the shelf, however, it falls short on three fronts. It is not formal: with no structured, searchable statement of the problem, the search has little structure to exploit and hard constraints are not guaranteed. It is not transferable: each task is solved from scratch, so nothing learned on one task carri
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of designing efficient datacenter control-plane policies, which is a complex and time-consuming task. The researchers built AtumAI, a framework that uses agentic AI to automate the policy design process. The result is a more efficient and structured approach to policy design.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage datacenter infrastructure, here is what to do: review your current policy design process, consider adopting AtumAI or similar frameworks to automate policy design, and evaluate the potential benefits of improved efficiency and structure in your control-plane policies.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a principled framework for agentic generation of datacenter control-plane policies. It addresses limitations of existing methods and has potential applications in datacenter management.

case_studies.abstract: Intent classification in Large Language Models (LLMs) involves categorizing user prompts into predefined classes. For instance, given a user prompt, the system must determine whether it primarily concerns mathematics, coding, or general text processing. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of intent classification in Large Language Models, where the authors built and compared training-free and training-based approaches to categorize user prompts into predefined classes, resulting in improved accuracy and computational efficiency. The study compared two lightweight, training-free methods and found they can be effective for intent classification. This research is relevant to natural language processing and AI model optimization.

case_studies.title: ACEM: A Cost Estimation Model for Agentic Software Engineering
case_studies.abstract: Traditional software cost estimation models, such as COCOMO II, Function Points, and Story Points, assume that development effort is primarily driven by human labor in design, coding, and testing. Agentic software engineering, where autonomous AI agents perform substantial implementation work and humans focus on planning, specification, and validation, challenges this assumption. New cost dimensions arise: large language model (LLM) token consumption across agent actions, Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) oversight effort, and infrastructure costs for agent orchestration and tooling. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inaccurate software cost estimation in projects that use autonomous AI agents, by building a new cost estimation model called ACEM, which resulted in a more accurate estimation of costs. The model considers new cost dimensions such as large language model token consumption and Human-in-the-Loop oversight effort. The research helps organizations better plan and budget for agentic software engineering projects.

case_studies.title: HALT: Verification-Aware Stopping for Retrieval-Augmented Search Agents
case_studies.abstract: Retrieval-augmented search agents answer multi-hop questions by repeatedly issuing search queries and accumulating evidence. This creates a stopping problem: after the necessary evidence has appeared, further retrieval often adds cost, latency, and distracting context rather than useful information. We frame stopping as evidence coverage rather than generator confidence, and introduce HALT, a lightweight verification-aware policy that leaves the search agent unchanged. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of stopping retrieval-augmented search agents from collecting unnecessary information, by introducing HALT, a verification-aware policy that stops the search agent when enough evidence is collected. The result is a more efficient search process with reduced cost and latency. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

However, the novelty is not directly applicable to current IT infrastructure, and the real-world impact is limited. The AI maturity is moderate due to the use of multi-hop QA and retrieval-augmented search agents. Monetization potential is low since the paper does not discuss commercial applications. case_studies.abstract: LLM-agent evaluations often produce task outcomes long before the full benchmark run is complete. A partial score is tempting to report, but it does not show whether the observed tasks support the same conclusion as the completed evaluation. Early tasks can omit important parts of a benchmark, running cheaper tasks first can distort the observed sample, and a rule that decides only easy pairs can appear accurate while leaving many comparisons unresolved. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) agents by introducing ParEvalLayer, a decision layer that assesses paired outcomes for two agent systems. It builds a system to support decisions based on partial evaluations, addressing the issue of incomplete or distorted results. The result is a more accurate comparison of LLM agents.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on evaluating LLM agents rather than managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Relevant to LLM-agent evaluations, which are used in various IT applications. Novel decision layer concept. Could be valuable for comparing AI models in IT infrastructures, with clear potential for use in real-world systems within 90 days.

case_studies.title: Why Large Language Models Fail at Tabular Prediction
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become the default tool for a remarkable range of tasks, yet they have had conspicuously little success at one of the most common machine learning workloads: predictive analytics over tabular data. This gap is the founding premise of the fast-growing field of tabular foundation models, but the question of why generic LLMs fail has remained open. case_studies.summary: This research identifies why large language models struggle with predictive analytics on tabular data, finding that they fail to make accurate predictions despite being proficient in other areas. The authors studied a state-of-the-art language model to understand this limitation. The result highlights a gap in the capabilities of current language models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on the limitations of large language models in predictive analytics rather than cloud infrastructure management or maintenance.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Low novelty and relevance due to academic nature and focus on LLM's limitations rather than practical application. Limited value within 90 days as the paper does not provide actionable steps for implementation or improvement.

case_studies.title: Agentic Incident Response through Digital Twin-Enhanced Multiscale Planning
case_studies.abstract: Incident response is currently managed by security operators using predefined playbooks, resulting in slow, labor-intensive security decision-making processes. Decision-theoretic approaches based on control, optimization, and reinforcement learning have been proposed to automate such planning tasks with well-grounded approaches, yet most of which, while guaranteeing strong performance, are limited to abstract models and cannot be directly applied to operational systems. case_studies.summary: This research aims to improve incident response by automating planning tasks, creating a digital twin-enhanced multiscale planning system to speed up security decision-making. The result is a more efficient and automated approach to incident response. This could help IT teams respond to security incidents more quickly.

case_studies.title: Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories
case_studies.abstract: Agents built around large language models continually accumulate interaction trajectories during deployment, yet their behavior typically remains fixed. Beyond updating model weights, these trajectories can improve the agent harness that constructs context, mediates tools, validates actions, and recovers execution. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of improving the agent harness in large language models by learning from failure trajectories. The researchers built Harness-R1, a method that enables editing of an existing executable runtime using online reinforcement learning. The result is a learned capability that optimizes edits to the harness.

case_studies.title: Homebot: A Personal AI Agent for Conversational Home Assistance and Automation
case_studies.abstract: \texttt{Homebot} is a locally deployable AI agent for conversational household assistance and automation. It accepts voice and instant-messaging requests through a shared runtime that combines language-model responses with registered tools and task-specific skills. The design separates common request processing from session ownership: messaging history remains scoped to a channel and chat, whereas voice interaction is bounded by wake-word activation. case_studies.summary: Homebot is a personal AI agent that solves the problem of household automation by allowing users to control devices and access information through voice and instant-messaging requests. The researchers built a locally deployable AI agent that combines language-model responses with registered tools and task-specific skills. The result is a conversational home assistance system that can be controlled hands-free.
